paragraphs: The move from the state of nature to the civil state changes man in a remarkable way. Justice replaces instinct in his conduct, and his actions take on the morality they lacked before. Only then, when the voice of duty replaces physical impulse and right replaces appetite, does _man_, who until now had thought only of himself, find that he must act on different principles and consult his reason before following his inclinations. In this state he gives up some of the advantages nature gave him, but he gains far greater ones. His faculties are exercised and developed, his ideas broadened, his feelings elevated, and his whole soul lifted so high that, if the abuses of this new condition did not so often drag him below the one he left, he would have to bless forever the happy moment that pulled him out of it, and that turned him from a stupid, unimaginative animal into an intelligent being and a man.

Let us add up the whole account in terms that are easy to compare. By the social compact, man loses his natural liberty and his unlimited right to anything he tries to get and manages to get. He gains civil liberty and ownership of everything he possesses. To weigh one against the other without error, we must keep several distinctions clear. Natural liberty is bounded only by the strength of the individual, while civil liberty is limited by the general will. And possession is merely the result of force or of the right of the first occupier, while property can be founded only on a positive title.

Besides all this, we could add moral liberty to what man gains in the civil state. Moral liberty alone makes him truly his own master, since being driven by appetite alone is slavery, while obeying a law we prescribe for ourselves is liberty. But I have already said too much on this subject, and the philosophical meaning of the word liberty is not our concern here.
